name: Run and review daily quality control (community laboratory analysers and microbiology instruments)
summary: Before an analyser may report patient results each day, technologists run control materials with known values, and quality control software checks them against statistical rules. If a control fails, the assay is held, the control is usually repeated, and the technologist troubleshoots, recalibrates or calls vendor service, decides whether released patient results need a look-back and documents the event. Charge technologists review each analyser's QC weekly and a quality specialist and the laboratory manager review monthly statistics against peer laboratories. Most elapsed time is waiting for instrument runs, later shifts and periodic reviews; the costly parts are failures, which happen on roughly one analyser-day in five and are often first met by repeating the control.

baseline.org_archetype: A large Canadian community laboratory company with nine accredited laboratories, track-connected chemistry and haematology lines, automated microbiology instruments and commercial QC software with peer comparison.
baseline.notes: About 150 test systems run QC each day across the laboratories (4,500 analyser-days a month in the organisation file), about four fifths in the core laboratory and one fifth in microbiology.

trigger: The analyser's daily start-up maintenance is logged complete and the first scheduled QC event of the day falls due.
end_state: Every QC event of the analyser-day is accepted or documented with corrective action, and the day's QC record is signed in the supervisor's weekly review (and, for the month-end day, in the monthly review).

volume.seasonality: Nearly flat; some single-shift analysers and microbiology benches do not run on Sundays and holidays.

evidence.note: Taken from the organisation file process map (about 150 test systems a day); the analyser count is the organisation file author's estimate.

steps.name: Flag QC due after daily maintenance
steps.description: When the technologist logs the analyser's daily start-up maintenance as complete, the middleware and QC software mark the scheduled QC event as due and keep patient testing for that analyser on hold until QC is accepted.

next.condition: chemistry, immunoassay, haematology, coagulation or urinalysis analyser

evidence.note: QC before patient testing each day and after maintenance is described; the 80/20 split between core and microbiology test systems is an estimate.

steps.name: Prepare control materials
steps.description: The technologist takes the control vials for each level from the refrigerator or freezer, thaws or reconstitutes them, mixes them, checks the open-vial expiry and lot number, and pours them into barcoded sample cups or tubes.

error.defect_description: Wrong level or lot loaded, expired or poorly mixed material, or material left out too long.

evidence.note: User errors with control material are named as the first thing to rule out; hands-on minutes are an estimate.

steps.name: Load controls and request the QC run
steps.description: The technologist places the control cups in the analyser's QC rack or track input, confirms the analyser reads each barcode and has ordered the right tests for every level, and starts the run.

error.defect_description: Control placed in the wrong position or tests not ordered for a level.

evidence.note: Ordinary analyser operation; minutes estimated from common practice.

steps.name: Analyser measures the controls
steps.description: The analyser aspirates and measures each control level for every assay on board; nobody works on the case while the instrument runs, and patient tubes queue behind the hold.

evidence.note: Instrument run time of 10 to 45 minutes for a full control set is an estimate; treated as waiting because no one is working.

steps.name: Apply QC rules and peer statistics
steps.description: The middleware passes control results to the QC software, which plots them on Levey-Jennings charts, applies the configured Westgard rules for each assay and level, and locks any assay that breaks a rejection rule.

evidence.note: Multirule logic and the company's QC monitoring software are described.

steps.name: Review QC and accept or reject the run
steps.description: The technologist opens the QC software, checks every assay and level for warnings and rejections, looks at the trend on the Levey-Jennings chart, and either accepts the run so patient testing and autoverification resume or rejects the failing assay.

error.defect_description: A real shift accepted because a 1-2s warning was ignored.

control.basis: Ontario licensing requires the IQMH quality management program and accreditation to ISO 15189; QC must be acceptable before patient results are released (CLSI C24 practice, Westgard multirule)

next.condition: accepted; the analyser runs evening or night shifts with further QC events
accepted; single QC event for the day
one or more assays break a rejection rule

evidence.note: Ontario licensed laboratories must be in the accreditation and proficiency testing program. 29% of US laboratories report being out of control more than once a day and 1-2s rules falsely reject 9% to 14% of good runs; a 13% rejection rate for the first QC event of an analyser-day is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Hold the assay and repeat the control
steps.description: The technologist suspends reporting and autoverification for the failed assay, checks for obvious causes such as the wrong level, expired material or a bubble, and repeats the control with a fresh aliquot or a new vial.

error.defect_description: A repeat that falls inside limits by chance hides a real systematic error.

control.basis: CLSI C24 out-of-control procedure under the ISO 15189 accredited quality management system: stop reporting, find and correct the cause, rerun QC before resuming

next.condition: repeat in control; judged random error

evidence.note: Nearly 90% of US laboratories repeat the control first; the share resolved by the repeat is an estimate.

steps.name: Troubleshoot the failing assay
steps.description: The technologist reviews the Levey-Jennings chart for a shift or trend, checks reagent lot and onboard stability, calibration age and recent maintenance, compares with a second analyser or peer data, and decides whether to recalibrate, change reagent or call for service.

error.defect_description: Wrong cause chosen, leading to an unnecessary recalibration.

control.basis: CLSI C24 out-of-control procedure under the ISO 15189 accredited quality management system: stop reporting, find and correct the cause, rerun QC before resuming

next.condition: recalibration or new reagent pack likely to fix it
hardware fault or cause not found

evidence.note: Troubleshooting steps are described; the wait is the repeat control run time; minutes and branch shares are estimates.

steps.name: Recalibrate or change reagent and rerun all levels
steps.description: The technologist loads calibrators or a new reagent pack, runs and accepts the calibration, then reruns every control level for the assay and checks them against the rules before releasing the hold.

error.defect_description: Calibration accepted with a calibrator handling error.

control.basis: CLSI C24 out-of-control procedure under the ISO 15189 accredited quality management system: stop reporting, find and correct the cause, rerun QC before resuming

evidence.note: Controls after recalibration, reagent change or major maintenance are required before patient testing resumes; branch shares are estimates.

steps.name: Escalate and call vendor technical support
steps.description: The charge technologist reviews what was tried, takes the assay or analyser out of service, moves its work to a backup analyser, and calls the vendor's technical support line or books a field service visit.

evidence.note: Rerouting to an instrument with acceptable QC and downtime costs are described; minutes and branch shares are estimates.

steps.name: Vendor field engineer repairs the analyser
steps.description: The instrument manufacturer's field service engineer arrives, diagnoses and repairs the analyser and leaves a service report; the analyser stays out of service until the technologist recalibrates and QC passes.

next.condition: repair complete; recalibrate and run QC

evidence.note: Response within the same day to two days is an estimate of common vendor service levels.

steps.name: Decide whether patient results need a look-back
steps.description: The charge technologist compares the failure time with the last acceptable QC, the size of the shift against the allowable error, and whether patient results were released in between, then either closes the event or asks the core laboratory to retest stored specimens.

control.basis: CLSI C24 and ISO 15189: evaluate patient results since the last acceptable QC and correct reports when differences exceed the laboratory director's limits

evidence.note: Evaluating results since the last acceptable QC is described; retesting itself is in the core testing workflow.

steps.name: Document the event and corrective action
steps.description: The technologist enters the cause, the action taken and the repeat results as comments on the QC chart, updates the reagent and calibration logs, and releases the assay hold in the middleware.

error.defect_description: Corrective action not recorded or recorded without a cause.

control.basis: ISO 15189 records of QC and corrective action, reviewed at accreditation and IQMH assessment

next.condition: patient results affected, repeated failure or long downtime

evidence.note: Documentation of every control procedure and corrective action is described; the nonconformance share is an estimate sized so QC failures supply about a quarter of the nonconformance process volume.

steps.name: Log a nonconformance in the QMS
steps.description: The charge technologist opens a nonconformance record in the quality management system, describes the QC failure, its effect on patient results and the immediate action, and routes it to quality assurance for root cause and corrective action.

control.basis: ISO 15189 nonconformity and corrective action management

evidence.note: Reporting nonconformities is a listed technologist duty and the QMS includes corrective action; minutes are estimates.

steps.name: Run and review the later QC events of the day
steps.description: For analysers that run evening and night shifts, the technologist on that shift prepares and loads the controls again at the scheduled interval or after a reagent change, and reviews and accepts the results in the QC software.

error.defect_description: Later QC event skipped or done late.

control.basis: Ontario licensing requires the IQMH quality management program and accreditation to ISO 15189; QC must be acceptable before patient results are released (CLSI C24 practice, Westgard multirule)

evidence.note: 53.7% of European laboratories run controls two or three times a day and C24 gives a 12-hour interval as an example; touch time and failure share are estimates.

steps.name: Run daily microbiology checks and controls
steps.description: The microbiology technologist records incubator temperatures and CO2, stains the Gram control slide, runs the MALDI-TOF calibration standard and molecular panel controls, and on scheduled days subcultures the reference strains for susceptibility QC.

error.defect_description: Control strain from an old subculture or wrong stain control used.

control.basis: ISO 15189 and CAP or MANQAP microbiology checklists: stains checked each day of use, media and susceptibility QC with reference strains

evidence.note: Daily stain checks, media checks and QC duties are described; the item list and minutes are estimates.

steps.name: Read and record the microbiology control results
steps.description: The technologist reads the Gram control reactions, the MALDI-TOF calibration score and the molecular control validity, records them in the QC log, and releases the bench for patient work.

control.basis: Ontario licensing requires the IQMH quality management program and accreditation to ISO 15189; QC must be acceptable before patient results are released (CLSI C24 practice, Westgard multirule)

next.condition: susceptibility QC strains set up today

evidence.note: Read times and the share of days with susceptibility QC are estimates.

steps.name: Read susceptibility QC strains after incubation
steps.description: After overnight incubation the technologist reads the reference strain results from the susceptibility instrument or disk plates and compares each drug with the published QC ranges before accepting the panel lot for patient reporting.

control.basis: Ontario licensing requires the IQMH quality management program and accreditation to ISO 15189; QC must be acceptable before patient results are released (CLSI C24 practice, Westgard multirule)

next.condition: one or more drugs out of range

evidence.note: Overnight incubation of 16 to 24 hours and out-of-range share are estimates from common practice.

steps.name: Investigate a microbiology QC failure
steps.description: The technologist checks the strain's subculture generation, inoculum density, media and card lots and instrument logs, repeats the QC, and holds or comments the affected patient results until the repeat passes.
outputs: hold or comment on patient results

control.basis: CLSI C24 out-of-control procedure under the ISO 15189 accredited quality management system: stop reporting, find and correct the cause, rerun QC before resuming

next.condition: patient results affected or repeated failure

evidence.note: Common practice; minutes and branch shares are estimates.

steps.name: Review the week's QC for the analyser
steps.description: The charge technologist opens the analyser's QC charts and event log for the past week, checks that every run was accepted or documented with a corrective action, signs the review electronically and returns incomplete entries to the bench.

control.basis: Documented periodic QC review by a supervisor (every 7 to 10 days under some accreditation checklists)

evidence.note: A documented review every 7 to 10 days is described; minutes per analyser-day are an estimate.

steps.name: Review an analyser-day with a logged event
steps.description: In the weekly review the charge technologist reads the event documentation and the linked nonconformance, checks that any look-back was completed and corrected reports were issued, and signs the review.

control.basis: Documented periodic QC review by a supervisor

evidence.note: Review of corrective actions is described; minutes are estimates.

steps.name: Review the week's microbiology QC log
steps.description: The charge technologist checks the microbiology QC and temperature logs for the week, confirms failures were investigated and repeated, and signs the log.

control.basis: Documented periodic QC review by a supervisor

evidence.note: Periodic documented review is described; minutes are estimates.

steps.name: Complete missing QC documentation
steps.description: The technologist who ran the QC adds the missing cause, action or initials to the QC chart or log after the charge technologist returns it, and the record is re-signed.

evidence.note: Return of incomplete records is common practice; share and minutes are estimates.

steps.name: Compile monthly QC statistics and peer comparison
steps.description: After month end the quality specialist exports each assay's monthly mean, SD and CV from the QC software, compares them with the peer group report, and flags assays with drift, bias or rising imprecision for the laboratory manager.

evidence.note: Peer group comparison and review of months of QC data are described; minutes per analyser-month are estimates.

steps.name: Review and sign the monthly QC summary
steps.description: The laboratory manager reads the monthly summary, agrees actions such as new target ranges, recalibration schedules or a service call, and signs the review as the director's designee.

control.basis: Monthly review of QC data by the laboratory director or designee (accreditation checklist requirement)

evidence.note: Director approval of control ranges is described; the monthly cadence follows common accreditation checklists; minutes are estimates.

exceptions.name: Rejected run resolved by a repeat control
exceptions.description: The repeat falls inside limits and the event is documented as random error; common in practice although C24 discourages repeating without investigation.

exceptions.name: Recalibration or reagent change
exceptions.description: The repeat still fails; the technologist troubleshoots, recalibrates and reruns all levels, and the charge technologist decides on a look-back.

exceptions.name: Analyser down for vendor service
exceptions.description: Troubleshooting fails; the charge technologist moves work to a backup analyser and a field engineer repairs the instrument before QC is rerun.

exceptions.name: Microbiology QC failure
exceptions.description: A stain, identification or susceptibility control fails and is investigated and repeated; affected patient results are held or commented.

exceptions.name: Incomplete documentation returned
exceptions.description: The weekly reviewer finds a missing corrective action or initials and returns the record.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from the first QC event of the analyser-day to the supervisor's signed review
benchmarks.population: Author's estimate for a laboratory that reviews QC weekly

evidence.note: Derived from the 7 to 10 day documented review interval described in clp_qcproc: a day's record waits on average about half a week for the review.

benchmarks.unit: percent of US laboratories reporting out-of-control events more than once a day
percent of US laboratories whose first response to a QC flag is to repeat the control

evidence.note: Stated as nearly 90%.

benchmarks.unit: percent of good runs rejected using 2 SD limits with two controls

pain_points.description: Repeating a failed control until it passes is the most common first response and can hide a real shift, so look-backs and corrected reports come later than they should.

evidence.note: Nearly 90% of US laboratories repeat first; C24 practice says to investigate and evaluate patient results.

pain_points.description: Wide 2 SD limits on many assays create false rejections that consume troubleshooting time and reagent.

evidence.note: 9% to 14% false rejection with 2 SD limits; 73% of US labs use 2 SD limits on all tests.

pain_points.description: Corrective action notes are often incomplete and are only caught in the weekly review, days after the event.

evidence.note: Common audit finding; share is an estimate.

pain_points.description: Vendor field service waits keep an analyser down for hours to days and push work to backup analysers with manual review.

evidence.note: Downtime and rerouting are described as failure costs.

sources.title: Top ten findings of the 2021 Global QC Survey
sources.supports: 29% of US laboratories are out of control more than once a day; nearly 90% of US laboratories repeat the control as the first response (57% in Latin and South America); 53.7% of European laboratories run controls two or three times a day; Westgard rules used on some or all tests by 76% of US laboratories; about two thirds of laboratories have not changed QC to reduce cost; 3% of US laboratories report patient results despite a QC failure.

sources.title: The 7 best practices to recover from an out-of-control event
sources.supports: Steps based on CLSI C24: stop patient reporting and turn off autoverification for the assay, reroute samples to an instrument with acceptable QC, rule out user error (wrong level, lot, volume, material left out), review Levey-Jennings charts and recent calibration, reagent lot or maintenance changes, correct the cause and resume only when QC passes, re-test patient samples run since the last acceptable QC against limits set by the laboratory director, issue corrected reports, document root cause and corrective and preventive action.

sources.title: 42 CFR 493.1256 Standard: Control procedures
sources.publisher: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School
sources.supports: US rule used as a reference for common practice: two control materials of different concentration once each day of testing for quantitative tests, positive and negative controls for qualitative tests, controls before resuming patient testing after a reagent change or major maintenance, control results must meet criteria before patient results are reported, stains checked each day of use, media checked for sterility and growth, all control procedures documented.

sources.title: Westgard Rules: multirule QC
sources.supports: Multirule QC: 1-2s is a warning rule that triggers inspection; 1-3s, 2-2s, R-4s, 4-1s and 10x are rejection rules; with 2s limits about 9% (two controls) to 14% (three controls) of good runs are falsely rejected, against about 1% for 1-3s.

sources.title: Exploring cost of quality in the lab (Quintenz and Williams)
sources.supports: Failure costs include invalid instrument runs, rework and retesting, downtime, troubleshooting, documentation and supervision time; external failures include report recalls and complaints; QC run once a day is the usual frequency in the worked example.

sources.title: How to improve laboratory quality control processes (MacCormack)
sources.supports: Some accreditation organisations require documented review of QC every 7 to 10 days; laboratories review at least three months of daily QC data to set ranges; the laboratory director approves new control ranges; drifts and shifts are found by reviewing Levey-Jennings charts.

sources.title: Standards of practice
sources.publisher: Canadian Society for Medical Laboratory Science
sources.supports: MLTs adhere to quality control protocols, review abnormal QC results, troubleshoot equipment malfunctions and validate test results; laboratory assistants work on pre- and post-analytical specimen handling and prepare reagents.

sources.title: Laws and legislation governing MLT practice
sources.publisher: College of Medical Laboratory Technologists of Ontario
sources.supports: Medical Laboratory Technology Act, 1991: the scope of practice is the performance of laboratory investigations and the evaluation of the technical sufficiency of the investigations and their results; communicating a diagnosis is not an MLT authorised act; protected title.

sources.title: Licences and quality commitment
sources.supports: The quality management system uses software to monitor quality control of analytical processes, external quality assessment (CAP, QMP-LS, Healthmetrix) for all assays, internal audits and document control; Brampton, London, Ottawa and Peterborough hold ISO 15189 accreditation and Ontario licences; Winnipeg holds CAP and MANQAP accreditation for chemistry, cytology, histology, haematology and microbiology; pathology subspecialties include dermatopathology, gastrointestinal, uropathology, breast and gynaecologic pathology.

sources.supports: Ontario licensed laboratories must take part in a quality management program of accreditation and proficiency testing; community laboratory performance measures for 2016/17 (specimen rejection 0.9% and 0.2%, routine results within target 94% and 99%). assumptions: The process map names the maintenance record from fac-instrument-maintenance as the trigger; in practice the calendar starts each analyser-day, and the logged daily start-up maintenance is used as the trigger to match the map.
About 80% of analyser-days are core laboratory test systems and 20% microbiology instruments and benches; the organisation file does not give the split.

A rejected first QC event on 13% of core analyser-days and on 10% of later events gives about 19% of core analyser-days with at least one failure. This is the author's estimate, consistent with surveys showing many large laboratories out of control daily.
When a failure occurs, the remaining QC events of that day are not modelled again; this slightly understates hands-on time on failure days.

Retesting of stored patient specimens in a look-back, holding of patient tubes and backup analyser runs are counted in the core testing workflow (steps s19 to s24 there), not here, to avoid double counting. Troubleshooting minutes spread across requisitions in that workflow overlap partly with steps s07 to s09 here.

Service calls go to fac-instrument-maintenance, but the process map lists no maintenance_request output for this process, so none is declared; the core testing workflow declares it on its analyser fault outcome.

The weekly supervisor review (amortised per analyser-day) and the monthly review (charged to the month-end day, one day in 30) are included, so cycle time is dominated by the wait for review rather than by the QC runs themselves.
Control frequency, rules and review cadence follow common accreditation practice under ISO 15189, IQMH and CAP; the US CLIA text is used only as a public description of the same practice.
Loaded costs are the organisation file's (hourly wage times 1.35).
